etymologies.etymologyHTML: From French contraster, from Italian contrastare (“to resist", "to withstand”), from Vulgar Latin *contrāstāre, from Latin contrā (“against”) + stō, stāre (“to stand”).

definitions.definition: (countable) A control on a television, etc, that adjusts the amount of contrast in the images being displayed.

quote.citation: 2009 May 4, Michael Chapman; Matthew Chapman, “Hremail #7”, in Homestar Runner‎[1], spoken by Strong Bad (Matthew Chapman):
quote.text: Ohh, you can't fool me. This thing's top of the line! It's got two contrast knobs!

definitions.definition: (countable) A difference in lightness, brightness and/or hue between two colours that makes them more or less distinguishable.
(countable) A difference between two objects, people or concepts.

quote.citation: 1908, W[illiam] B[lair] M[orton] Ferguson, chapter I, in Zollenstein, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: The colonel and his sponsor made a queer contrast: Greystone [the sponsor] long and stringy, with a face that seemed as if a cold wind was eternally playing on it.
... there is no quality in this world that is not what it is merely by contrast.

definitions.definition: (countable) Something that is opposite of or strikingly different from something else.

quote.citation: 2001, David L. Lieber, Jules Harlow, Etz Hayim: Torah and Commentary, page 746:
quote.text: Why this denunciation of idolatry at this point? And why are Shabbat and the sanctuary mentioned as contrasts to idol worship?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To set in opposition in order to show the difference or differences between; to counterpoint.

quote.citation: 1845, Charles Lyell, Lyell's Travels in North America:
quote.text: The joints which divide the sandstone contrast finely with the divisional planes which separate the basalt into pillars.
